title: Self-sufficiency or fatigue – scenarios to bookend European defence spending outlook
author: Keith Mason
text:
RESEARCH BRIEFING

16 Sep 2026

Self-sufficiency or fatigue – scenarios to bookend European defence spending outlook

We model two scenarios that bookend the EU’s defence spending outlook – a rapid push for self-sufficiency and a pullback driven by spending fatigue – and what each means for growth, debt, and borrowing costs.

The EU's defence spending ramp-up carries real consequences for growth, fiscal positions, and borrowing costs, but the range of possible outcomes is wide. We model two scenarios to bookend this uncertainty: a rapid drive for defence self-sufficiency, and a scenario where spending fatigue sets in. Neither scenario moves medium-term GDP dramatically – growth ends up 0.1-0.2 percentage points higher or lower over the next three years – but the self-sufficiency path puts considerably more strain on Europe's public finances.

In the self-sufficiency scenario, European NATO countries need to close a €1tn gap in equipment and personnel to reduce reliance on the US – €400bn more than our baseline already assumes. Despite the scale of this spending, the lift to GDP is modest and front-loaded, since defence multipliers are low and the need for speed pushes more of the spending into imports. The fiscal cost is steeper: long-term bond yields rise by 40-50 basis points in the most fiscally stretched countries, including Italy and Spain, though EU-level funding could help cap the increase.

The fatigue scenario paints a different picture. An end to the Russia-Ukraine war and a wave of European elections could push defence spending down governments' priority lists, with weaker public backing prompting some countries to cut expenditure by 0.5-1% of GDP by 2028. This would shave around 0.2 percentage points off Eurozone growth over the next two years, with the sharpest pullback in southern European countries furthest from Russia.
